summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections exist for sexual orientation or gender identity anywhere in the national framework. Legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition.

Criminalisation operates at more than one level. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids: on 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands in either direction, and the province-specific source reviewed yielded no usable finding on trans safety. The national score therefore applies without adjustment.

Three further indicators of the surrounding climate are on record. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality "morally unacceptable".
tangentialFactors:
The immediate turbulence is vigilante rather than judicial. Reporting from August 2026 ties the October 2025 presidential framing of LGBTQ+ people as a monitored risk directly to a wave of mob attacks on transgender women, so the practical danger a trans visitor faces may come from crowds and neighbourhood enforcement rather than from a court file.

Social hostility is measured at 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality morally unacceptable in a 2025 Pew figure, which sets the background against which visibility, disclosure and police complaints are weighed. The figure concerns homosexuality rather than transgender identity specifically, and no equivalent measurement for gender identity is available in the sources.

The pattern elsewhere in Indonesia is the useful comparison. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex activity under their own provisions, Aceh's punishments reach foreign visitors present in its territory, and the June 2025 Puncak villa raid shows that gatherings can be broken up on the basis of anonymous complaints even where, in Amnesty International's assessment, no law was broken. Bangka-Belitung Islands has no documented equivalent, but neither is there any documented local restraint.

The Constitutional Court's 5-4 refusal on 14 December 2017 to criminalise gay sex indicates a limit on legislative expansion, while the same court's earlier handling of gender-identity petitions and the surgical-and-judicial requirement for legal recognition point the other way. Protection machinery exists in form and has not been used to extend rights.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bangka-Belitung Islands live under the same national code as visitors, with no provincial protection on sexual orientation or gender identity and no hate-crime provision to invoke after an assault. A complaint about a mob attack would proceed as an ordinary assault case.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery and a judicial approval, a route that requires both medical intervention and a court process. Until it is completed, identity documents continue to carry the sex assigned at birth, which affects banking, employment, travel documents and any interaction with officials that checks gender markers.

No form of same-sex relationship carries legal standing: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are all unrecognised nationally, so residents have no next-of-kin, inheritance, hospital-visitation or property claim through a same-sex partner. The extra-marital sex provision in force since 2 January 2026 exposes people in long-term same-sex relationships to the same exposure as anyone else, with prosecutions reported as selective rather than systematic.

Residents also face the national security framing introduced by the October 2025 presidential decree, which places LGBTQ+ people within defence policy as a category to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 links that framing to vigilante attacks on transgender women.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty for sex outside marriage is stated as up to one year's imprisonment in the source inventory reviewed here, while the parent framework text for Indonesia records up to two years. The discrepancy is unresolved and neither figure has been reconciled against the text of the 2022 penal code.

No source in the inventory reports any trans-specific incident, arrest, raid, local bylaw or protective measure in Bangka-Belitung Islands itself. The province-specific reference reviewed produced no usable finding on trans safety, so the absence of documented local enforcement is not evidence that enforcement does not occur.

Whether any district-level religious bylaws with application to visitors are in force in Bangka-Belitung Islands is not sourced here. Only Aceh and South Sumatra are recorded as having their own criminalisation provisions.

The 93% Pew figure measures attitudes to homosexuality, not to transgender people, and no comparable measurement of attitudes to gender identity appears in the inventory. The frequency and outcome of prosecutions under the extra-marital sex provision since 2 January 2026 are likewise not quantified in these sources.
